Promotion and protection of human rights: the implications of the Cbdh’s accreditation to “A” status

By Joel TOKPONOU, 17 May 2022 at 10:16

The members of the Beninese Human Rights Commission (Cbdh) presented to the media, yesterday Monday 16 May, the implications and prospects of the institution’s accreditation to United Nations “A” status. It was also an opportunity to take stock of 40 months of activity.

It took the Beninese Human Rights Commission (Cbdh) less than 40 months to obtain accreditation to “A” status from the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions. This achievement, announced on 29 March, is an expression of recognition of the actions carried out by the team of Isidore Clément Capo-Chichi, president of the Cbdh.

“From now on, Benin will be able to sit at the same table as the so-called great democracies,” says Emerico Adjovi, a member of the Cbdh, with satisfaction.

To get there, several indicators were assessed. But those that triggered the evaluation process are principally the institution’s financial autonomy, the possession of a headquarters where citizens can go to lodge complaints, and the creation of regional branches with a view to proximity to potential complainants, wherever they may be on the national territory. On this last point, the Cbdh has been able to open six branches, namely in Lokossa, Abomey, Porto-Novo, Parakou, Natitingou and in the Atlantique department, thanks to the “Advancing Rights in Benin Activity” project funded by the American Bar Association. “Our ambition, in the future, is to manage to open the other branches in the remaining departments. In the long term, we plan to cover all 77 communes,” says Isidore Clément Capo-Chichi.

But in the meantime, this accreditation allows the Cbdh “to take the floor before the United Nations in its field of competence. The imminent experience is the Universal Periodic Review (UPR), which will be held in January 2023. Following the government, the president of the Cbdh will speak before the United Nations Human Rights Council, where Benin sits.”

“A” accreditation is also proof of the commitment to continue to respect the obligations of international human rights law.

But the president of the Cbdh makes an important clarification. The accreditation is not permanent. It is assessed every five years and the country can lose it when one of the accreditation criteria is missing. This qualification takes nothing away from the determination of the Cbdh, which can count on its partners. The president moreover expressed his gratitude to the American Bar Association, to USAID and to the embassy of the United States, which support the institution in its actions. The government too received praise for having “placed its trust in men it did not choose but appointed”.

An instructive record

The presentation of the implications of “A” accreditation was also an opportunity for the members of the Cbdh to give a brief overview of their institution’s record. And the least one can say is that the harvest is abundant. To the institution’s credit, one already notes the publication of two reports, all of which were presented to the President of the Republic and then to the deputies of the National Assembly in accordance with law 2012-36 of 15 February 2013 establishing the Beninese Human Rights Commission (Cbdh) in the Republic of Benin.

Also to be noted in the record is the drawing up of a five-year national youth strategy.

In the same dynamic of promoting and protecting human rights, the Cbdh has carried out actions in collaboration with civil society organisations (CSOs) and other non-governmental organisations.

Faced with this record, the representatives of the CSOs, of the youth organisations, of USAID and of the embassy of the United States of America unanimously welcomed the results obtained. In particular, the technical and financial partners assured the Cbdh that their support would continue.

a4136.t:
The Mozambican government and the United Nations announced here on Friday a 250-million-U.S. dollar humanitarian response plan for the 1.1 million people affected by terrorism in three northern provinces of the country.
The support is expected to supply the deficit indicated for the necessary contingency plan throughout 2021 to be applied in Cabo Delgado, Niassa and Nampula provinces.
The Director General of the National Institute for Disaster Management (INGC) Luisa Meque said at the launching ceremony that the people affected by terrorism in the country are still facing enormous challenges for the rapid normalization of their lives.
“So we urge everyone, within their possibilities, to continue to show their solidarity to the people affected, contributing with means and assets that allow for continued humanitarian assistance and rapid post-disaster reconstruction,” said Meque.
The United Nations Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator in Mozambique, Myrta Kaulard, also pointed out at the ceremony that every effort is needed to ensure a minimum decent life for the affected people.
“People were forced to leave their homes with nothing more than the clothes they wore. They lost their belongings, their livelihood, and their future. Humanitarian aid is vital to alleviate their suffering,” said Kaulard.
Terrorism in Cabo Delgado province poses a real threat to the country, with the potential to expand to other regions of the continent and the world, said the Mozambican foreign minister Veronica Macamo at the ceremony.
“Therefore, we are convinced that the ultimate solution to the problem also includes the involvement of the international community,” she said.
According to the government, about 80 percent of the displaced people who were farmers have stopped food producing, increasing the risk of food insecurity in the region.

a4272.t:
A four-year-old child became the second person to die of Ebola in Uganda since the outbreak was announced in late January, the World Health Organization said on Saturday.
On Tuesday, Ugandan health officials confirmed that the country had recorded 10 infections with the Sudan strain of the virus.
The death of the child is seen as a setback for health officials who had hoped the highly infectious disease had been “contained” after eight people had recovered following treatment.
The child passed away at the Mulago Hospital in the capital, Kampala, the only facility in the country for dealing with Ebola cases.
The first victim was a male nurse who died the day before the outbreak was declared on 30 January.
Symptoms of the often fatal disease include fever, headaches, muscle pains, and bleeding. The virus is transmitted through contact with infected bodily fluids and tissue.
Contract tracing is key to stemming the spread of Ebola and the WHO said it and others were working to strengthen this together with surveillance.
There are no approved vaccines for the Sudan strain, however a vaccination trial was launched in Uganda earlier this month
The WHO has given Uganda at least $3 million to support its Ebola response, but there are concerns about funding in the wake of the US administration’s decision to cut funding to USAID.
Uganda’s last outbreak, discovered in September 2022, killed at least 55 people before it was declared over in January 2023.
More than 15,000 people have died of Ebola in Africa in the past 50 years.
It was discovered in 1976 in simultaneous outbreaks in South Sudan and Congo, where it occurred in a village near the Ebola River, after which the disease is named.
Source: Africanews

a4284.t:
At a time the proposed K8 trillion 2025/26 National Budget is undergoing scrutiny, observers have said Treasury will be under pressure to balance funding for social services and productive sectors due to statutory obligations.
The stakeholders expressed the sentiments at a public hearing in Lilongwe on Wednesday on the proposed fiscal plan’s spending on social and productive sectors. The stakeholders and technocrats discussed how the budget responds to the two sectors.
The concerns come against the backdrop of data showing that in the proposed budget, the social services sector allocation has increased to 33 percent from 31 percent of the budget in the proposed fiscal plan.
The European Union and Unicef have commended this development, but highlighted that there are still more funding needs.
On the contrary, development budget allocation has dropped from 30 percent of the total budget in 2024/25 fiscal year to 27 percent of the proposed 2025/26 budget at K2 trillion.
During the discussions, some stakeholders said the social sector, which looks at child welfare, education, health and general social services should not be left out while others favoured the production sector which can generate money.
In his remarks, EU Ambassador Rune Skinnebach said although the production sector is key to fixing the country’s macroeconomic challenges such as balance of payments needs, social protection must not be neglected.
He said: “Social protection, whether it is education, health or social services in general, is necessary. Of course, there are dilemmas that are presented particularly in Malawi where there is limited fiscal space to do all the things right.
“You may say for us to be self-reliant, maybe we need to favour the productive sector, we need to promote exports, we need to limit imports, but to be successful, we need the people and the people are secured by social services.”
Skinnebach underscored the need to ensure the resources are optimally used by ensuring fiscal discipline, especially considering that this is an election year.
National Planning Commission director general Thomas Munthali said while not neglecting the social sector, there is a need for the government to fund production sectors that generate money to ensure sustainable social services.
He said with United States government terminating contracts worth $230.4 million (about K400 billion) under the United States Agency for International Development (USaid), there is a need for Malawi to be self-reliant by investing in productive sectors to generate money to sustain social services.
He said: “We are all here because of the social sector. It is a sector we cannot do without, but the social sector does not finance itself. It needs money that is generated elsewhere if not from donors, so we need to invest in the productive sector to ensure sustainability.
“Currently, 80 percent of the budget is already covering statutory obligations like salaries, wages, interest payment and pension, among others, meaning the fiscal space is already squeezed.”
Speaking during the opening of the meeting, Second Deputy Speaker of Parliament Aisha Adams Mambo urged the experts to have thorough discussions that will ensure the budget resources are equitably distributed and benefit all sectors.
“In most cases, technocrats do not make changes after proposals were given during such budget hearings, but I encourage them to consider taking on board the advice that will be made by various stakeholders to ensure the 2025/26 budget resources are effectively used,” she said.
Various stakeholders, including members of Parliament, officials from Treasury, Reserve Bank of Malawi, government ministries, departments and agencies and non-governmental organisations participated in the meeting.
Legislators are currently discussing the budget in clusters.

a4314.t:
Ethiopia is making significant strides towards food self-sufficiency, a critical endeavor that underpins national freedom and sovereignty. This ambitious push is exemplified by the remarkable increase in domestic wheat production, signaling a profound shift away from reliance on foreign aid.
Historically, Ethiopia was among the sub-Saharan African nations most dependent on external assistance, with wheat imports alone costing the country over $1 billion annually. This staggering figure was highlighted by Dr. Getachew Diriba, Senior Advisor to the Minister of Agriculture and Chief Coordinator of the Ethiopian Food System Transformation and Nutrition. However, through concerted efforts, Ethiopia is now actively rewriting this narrative.
The commitment to enhancing food security extends beyond just staple crops. Under the "Lemat Turufat" (Bounty of the Basket) initiative, the country recently introduced grandparent chickens—a first for Ethiopia. These high-yield poultry are now producing eggs, with distribution to communities well underway, further diversifying local food sources.
Dr. Ambissa Muleta, Coordinator for the Ethiopian Food System Transition and Healthy Food, emphasized the role of innovative agricultural practices in this transformation. He pointed to the "Kuta Getem” (cluster farming) method as a key strategy, where farmers collaboratively utilize various mechanized tools to boost their collective productivity.
These multifaceted initiatives are not only propelling Ethiopia from a state of dependence to one of productivity but are also seen as fundamental to safeguarding the nation's sovereignty and independence. The imperative of achieving food self-sufficiency is a top priority, crucial for breaking free from external reliance.
Ethiopia has been chosen to host the second UN Food Systems Summit, a testament to its leadership in this vital area in recognition of its homegrown reforms and impressive progress in ensuring food security and self-sufficiency.

a4343.t:
Mozambique’s government on Tuesday announced the allocation of €120 million for humanitarian assistance and the rehabilitation of public infrastructure destroyed by Cyclone Chido and Cyclone Dikeledi in the north of the country.
“The government has funding mechanisms available to deal with the damage caused, having analysed and approved at this session the response plan that amounts to eight billion meticais [around €120 million], which will form the basis for assistance interventions and the rehabilitation of destroyed public infrastructure,” said the spokesman for the cabinet, Inocêncio Impissa, after a meeting of that body in Maputo.
Cyclones Chido and Dikeledi hit northern Mozambique in December and January, with the greatest impact on the provinces of Cabo Delgado and Nampula, causing deaths and material damage with the destruction of public and private infrastructure.
Impissa also said that in the first phase the government would prioritise “immediate responses” to the needs of the affected provinces, promising to mobilise resources for “medium and long-term interventions.”
On 13 January, Dikeledi – a severe tropical cyclone – made landfall in Mozambique, causing at least 11 deaths and affecting another 250,000 people, including the destruction of almost 20,000 homes, according to the latest official assessment by the authorities.
Cyclone Chido, which hit Mozambique on 14 December, killed at least 120 people and affected 450,000 others.
Mozambique is considered one of the countries most severely affected by climate change in the world, facing cyclical floods and tropical cyclones during the rainy season, which runs from October to April.

a4548.t:
Vers la prise en compte des migrants et des « sans terre » dans le foncier
L’atelier de validation de la stratégie d’appui aux communes pour l’élaboration et la mise en œuvre des programmes sociaux prenant en compte les migrants et « les sans terre » se déroule depuis mercredi dernier à l’hôtel Ayélawadjê de Porto-Novo. L’ouverture dudit atelier a été présidée par le ministre de la décentralisation, de la gouvernance locale, de l’administration et de l’aménagement du territoire en présence du coordonnateur national de Mca-Bénin et de la représentante résident de Mcc (Millénium challenge corporation). 
L’atelier a réuni les chefs services affaires domaniales des communes de Dangbo, Klouékanmè, Sinendé, Allada, Ouéssè, Adja-Ouèrè, Kpomassè, Dassa, Gogounou, Agbangnizoun, les autorités en charge de la décentralisation et de l’aménagement du territoire, les élus locaux et les responsables en charge du foncier au niveau du Mca-Bénin (Millénium challenge account Bénin). Son objectif principal est l’étude et l’amendement des diagnostics et propositions contenus dans le document qui servira de bréviaire pour les différents appuis aux communes ainsi que l’élaboration d’un dialogue franc entre les autorités administratives, les élus locaux et les populations vulnérables. Celai devra également permettre la mise en œuvre des programmes sociaux qui prennent en compte les populations vulnérables ou migrants et « les sans terre ». Au cours de la cérémonie d’ouverture des travaux de l’atelier de validation, le préfet de l’Ouémé/Plateau a mis l’accent sur les potentialités agricoles que regorge la vallée de l’Ouémé et souligné combien il est important de sécuriser les terres en vue de favoriser l’investissement durable et sans risque. Il a également saisi l’opportunité pour exhorter les autorités compétentes surtout les chefs services affaires domaniales à accompagner les visions du projet « Accès au foncier » de Mca-Bénin. Le maire de la ville de Porto-Novo, M. Moukaram Océni a insisté sur le fait que le présent atelier permettra d’identifier des groupes vulnérables et l’établissement d’un nouveau rapport avec les élus locaux. Pour lui, cette vision est capitale pour la lutte contre l’extrême pauvreté. Il a salué le gouvernement américain qui a permis au Bénin de prendre de nouvelles dispositions pour relever un peu le niveau de vie des populations à travers le financement des activités du Mca-Bénin. La représentante résident de Mcc, Mme Lee Roussel a quant à elle saisi l’occasion pour rappeler les objectifs des Etats-Unis à travers l’initiative du Mca. Elle a souligné que le foncier constitue l’un des problèmes qui freinent l’émancipation des pays surtout ceux en voie de développement. Pour le coordonnateur national du Mca-Bénin M. Simon Pierre Adovèlandé, le présent atelier est la preuve de la mise en œuvre des engagements inscrits dans les protocoles d’accord du Bénin dans le cadre du foncier. Au nom de ces protocoles, des communes ont été dotées de mobiliers de bureaux et de matériels roulants qui peuvent leur permettre d’accompagner le Programme dans sa politique de sécurisation des terres par l’initiative des Plans fonciers ruraux (Pfr). Une quarantaine de communes est concernée par ce projet qui va s’étendre probablement à d’autres. Procédant à l’ouverture officielle de l’atelier, Alassane Séïdou a rappelé l’importance du document et a aussi tenu a remercié les Etats-Unis pour leur assistance. 
Après la cérémonie d’ouverture, des commissions ont été constituées pour les travaux qui devront s’achever ce jeudi 23 juillet 2009. Les participants ont à développer une vision de la stratégie d’appui aux communes pour élaborer et mettre en œuvre des programmes sociaux prenant en compte les migrants et les « sans terre » en validant de manière participative
Contexte général de l’atelier selon Mca-Bénin
Le gouvernement de la République du Bénin et le gouvernement des Etats-Unis d’Amérique, agissant par le biais du Millénium challenge corporation (Mcc) ont conclu un Accord visant la fourniture d’une assistance technique au Bénin en vue d’améliorer l’accès au foncier à ses citoyens. Le gouvernement béninois a crée l’agence dénommée Millénium challenge account (Mca-Bénin) chargée de gérer et d’exécuter les tâches relatives à l’assistance techniques définie dans l’Accord. L’objectif général dudit Accord est de stimuler la croissance des investissements et de promouvoir le secteur privé du Bénin, conditions fondamentales à une croissance économique et à une réduction de la pauvreté. Dans le cadre de l’Accord, les parties ont identifié des objectifs spécifiques au projet dont l’appui à l’élaboration d’une politique foncière et à la réforme de la législation sur le foncier, la formalisation des droits de propriété foncière et appui aux communes dans la gestion d’une nouveau régime foncier et l’amélioration du système d’enregistrement et de gestion de l’information foncière, l’élaboration d’activités d’information, l’éducation et de communication. Les activités d’appui aux communes prévoient la solution à deux problèmes cruciaux en matière de politique foncière. Dans certaines zones rurales du Bénin, dénommées zones ‘’hôtes’’, les migrants constituent une partie importante de la population. Toutefois, leur statut ne leur permet pas de faire des investissements durables dans les terres qu’ils occupent. Les droits fonciers qu’ils détiennent sont précaires, limités et révocables à tout moment.
Cette situation constitue une sérieuse entrave au développement de chaque économie locale et, en conséquence, à l’économie du pays en général. Dans d’autres zones périurbaines, des nombres croissants de paysans « sans terre » sont entrain de s’installer. Ces citoyens ruraux déplacés se disputent la terre qui est attrayante pour d’autres investissements. Le fait qu’ils manquent de biens et de qualifications professionnelles les rend potentiellement vulnérables et augmente les niveaux de pauvreté dans les communes périurbaines. C’est pourquoi les objectifs des services de cette consultation sont entre autres, l’élaborer d’une stratégie par laquelle Mca-Bénin peut appuyer les communes en adoptant et en mettant en œuvre des programmes sociaux qui prennent en compte les besoins des migrants et des personnes sans terre et l’application de la stratégie dans un groupe de communes sélectionnées.
Judicaël-Rock Hounwanou (Collaboration Le Matin/La Nouvelle Tribune)
a4548.en:
Toward taking migrants and the "landless" into account in land tenure

The workshop to validate the strategy of support to communes for the development and implementation of social programmes taking migrants and the "landless" into account has been taking place since last Wednesday at the Ayelawadje hotel in Porto-Novo. The opening of the said workshop was chaired by the Minister of Decentralisation, Local Governance, Administration and Territorial Planning, in the presence of the national coordinator of MCA-Benin and the resident representative of MCC (Millennium Challenge Corporation).

The workshop brought together the heads of land affairs services of the communes of Dangbo, Klouekanme, Sinende, Allada, Ouesse, Adja-Ouere, Kpomasse, Dassa, Gogounou and Agbangnizoun, the authorities in charge of decentralisation and territorial planning, local elected officials and those responsible for land matters at MCA-Benin (Millennium Challenge Account Benin). Its main objective is the study and amendment of the diagnoses and proposals contained in the document that will serve as a breviary for the various forms of support to communes, as well as the development of a frank dialogue between administrative authorities, local elected officials and vulnerable populations. This should also make possible the implementation of social programmes that take into account vulnerable populations or migrants and the "landless". During the opening ceremony of the validation workshop, the prefect of Oueme/Plateau stressed the agricultural potential of the Oueme valley and underlined how important it is to secure land in order to foster sustainable and risk-free investment. He also took the opportunity to urge the competent authorities, especially the heads of land affairs services, to support the vision of MCA-Benin's "Access to Land" project. The mayor of the city of Porto-Novo, Mr Moukaram Oceni, insisted that this workshop will make it possible to identify vulnerable groups and establish a new relationship with local elected officials. For him, this vision is crucial for the fight against extreme poverty. He praised the American government, which has enabled Benin to take new measures to raise the standard of living of the population somewhat through the financing of MCA-Benin's activities. The resident representative of MCC, Mrs Lee Roussel, for her part took the opportunity to recall the objectives of the United States through the MCA initiative. She underlined that land tenure is one of the problems hindering the emancipation of countries, especially developing ones. For the national coordinator of MCA-Benin, Mr Simon Pierre Adovelande, this workshop is proof of the implementation of the commitments set out in Benin's memoranda of understanding on land tenure. Under those protocols, communes have been provided with office furniture and rolling stock that can enable them to support the Programme in its policy of securing land through the initiative of Rural Land Plans (PFR). About forty communes are concerned by this project, which will probably be extended to others. Officially opening the workshop, Alassane Seidou recalled the importance of the document and also thanked the United States for their assistance.

After the opening ceremony, commissions were formed for the work, which was to conclude on Thursday 23 July 2009. Participants are to develop a vision of the strategy of support to communes to develop and implement social programmes taking migrants and the "landless" into account, validating it in a participatory manner.

General context of the workshop according to MCA-Benin

The government of the Republic of Benin and the government of the United States of America, acting through the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC), concluded an Agreement aimed at providing technical assistance to Benin with a view to improving its citizens' access to land. The Beninese government created the agency named Millennium Challenge Account (MCA-Benin), responsible for managing and executing the tasks relating to the technical assistance defined in the Agreement. The general objective of the said Agreement is to stimulate the growth of investment and promote Benin's private sector, fundamental conditions for economic growth and poverty reduction. Under the Agreement, the parties identified specific objectives for the project, including support for the development of a land policy and reform of land legislation, the formalisation of land ownership rights and support to communes in managing a new land regime, the improvement of the land information registration and management system, and the development of information, education and communication activities. The activities of support to communes provide for the solution of two crucial problems in land policy. In certain rural areas of Benin, called "host" zones, migrants make up a significant part of the population. However, their status does not allow them to make sustainable investments in the land they occupy. The land rights they hold are precarious, limited and revocable at any time.

This situation constitutes a serious obstacle to the development of each local economy and, consequently, to the country's economy in general. In other peri-urban areas, growing numbers of "landless" peasants are settling. These displaced rural citizens compete for land that is attractive for other investments. The fact that they lack assets and professional qualifications makes them potentially vulnerable and increases poverty levels in peri-urban communes. That is why the objectives of the services of this consultation include developing a strategy through which MCA-Benin can support communes in adopting and implementing social programmes that take into account the needs of migrants and landless people, and applying the strategy in a selected group of communes.

Judicael-Rock Hounwanou (Collaboration Le Matin/La Nouvelle Tribune)

a4558.t:
Damaskus (UNA/QNA) – Syrische Forscher und Wissenschaftler betonten, dass der arabisch-islamische Krisengipfel, der am Montag in Doha stattfindet, die Bedeutung der Stärkung einer einheitlichen arabischen und islamischen Haltung gegenüber der israelischen Aggression unterstreicht, die sich gegen die Wohnquartiere mehrerer Hamas-Führer in der Hauptstadt Doha richtete. Ziel sei es, der aggressiven israelischen Politik entgegenzutreten, die Unterstützung für das palästinensische Volk und seine Rechte zu stärken und Katars zentrale Rolle bei den Vermittlungsbemühungen seit Kriegsausbruch hervorzuheben.
In einer Erklärung gegenüber der Qatar News Agency (QNA) sagte Dr. Khaled Zaarour, Dekan der Fakultät für Medien an der Universität Damaskus, dass die Einberufung des Gipfels zu diesem Zeitpunkt erhebliche Auswirkungen habe. Er wies darauf hin, dass dieser unmittelbar nach der israelischen Aggression gegen eine Hamas-Residenz in Doha stattfand, was ein klares Indiz für die Bedeutung des Zeitpunkts und des Inhalts sei.
Er fügte hinzu: „Auf dem Gipfel herrschte Einigkeit darüber, die Aggression abzulehnen und zu verurteilen. Man betrachtet sie als einen entscheidenden Wendepunkt in der Reihe der israelischen Angriffe, da sie sich gegen ein Land richtete, das Verhandlungen führt und die Rolle des Vermittlers spielt.“
Dr. Zaarour erklärte, dass der Gipfel die Botschaft aussenden werde, dass in den arabischen Reihen Einigkeit herrsche und das arabische Herz gut schlage.
Er fügte hinzu, dass die Aggression Auswirkungen auf die arabischen und islamischen Positionen gehabt habe und die Falschheit der israelischen Argumentation, mit der die Angriffe gerechtfertigt werden sollten, offengelegt habe. Er betonte, dass die Positionen nicht vollständig seien, wenn sie nicht in praktische Schritte umgesetzt würden. Dazu gehörten ein vollständiger politischer und wirtschaftlicher Boykott sowie eine Neugestaltung der militärischen und politischen Bündnispläne, um die loyalsten und treuesten Verbündeten zu finden und die wirtschaftliche Macht und geografische Lage der arabischen Länder zur Stärkung ihrer Positionen zu nutzen.
Der Dekan der Fakultät für Medien an der Universität Damaskus stellte fest, dass die Aggression ein Versuch gewesen sei, Katars Rolle zu schwächen, sie aber tatsächlich gestärkt habe. Die Erklärungen der arabischen Botschafter vor der UN-Generalversammlung zeigten, dass Katar aus der Aggression gestärkt und einflussreicher hervorgegangen sei, was die Gerechtigkeit für die palästinensische Sache weiter stärken werde.
Dr. Zaarour wies darauf hin, dass sich die politische und diplomatische Reaktion darauf konzentrieren müsse, den Aggressor einzudämmen und seine Anschuldigungen aufzudecken, und nicht nur darauf, eine Wiederholung der Aggression zu verhindern.
In ähnlicher Weise äußerte sich der Politikwissenschaftler Omar Idlebi vom Harmoon Center for Studies, die Einberufung des Krisengipfels spiegele eine seltene Einigkeit in der arabischen und islamischen Haltung wider und sei ein klarer Ausdruck der Solidarität mit dem Staat Katar angesichts einer Aggression, die alle roten Linien überschreite.
Omar Idlebi erklärte, dass die Einberufung des Gipfels nach den politischen und diplomatischen Bemühungen Katars und den internationalen Verurteilungen die Entschlossenheit der teilnehmenden Länder widerspiegele, ihre Positionen zu koordinieren, um der aggressiven Politik Israels gegenüber dem palästinensischen Volk und anderen Ländern in der Region entgegenzutreten, das Leid der Palästinenser im Westjordanland hervorzuheben und die internationale Gemeinschaft zu ernsthaften Bemühungen zu drängen, die Zweistaatenlösung und das Recht des palästinensischen Volkes auf einen unabhängigen Staat wiederzubeleben.
Er fügte hinzu, dass die teilnehmenden Länder über verschiedene Einflussmöglichkeiten verfügten, um das gewünschte Ziel zu erreichen. Dazu gehöre vor allem wirtschaftlicher Einfluss, um einen spürbaren Einfluss auf die internationale Herangehensweise an regionale Probleme zu nehmen und die Toleranz gegenüber der israelischen Aggression zu beenden.
Er betonte, dass die katarische Diplomatie eine bemerkenswerte Fähigkeit im Umgang mit der Aggression bewiesen habe. Dies sei durch eine offizielle Erklärung geschehen, in der sie diese als eklatanten und verräterischen Angriff beschrieb, und durch umfangreiche diplomatische Bemühungen in den Hauptstädten und im Sicherheitsrat, Unterstützung für die Position Katars zu mobilisieren. Dies habe zur Forderung nach einem arabisch-islamischen Gipfel geführt, um geeignete Positionen und Reaktionen zu diskutieren und zu koordinieren und das palästinensische Volk bei seiner Konfrontation mit der israelischen Politik zu unterstützen.
Idlebi erklärte, dass es durch die Vermittlung Katars in Zusammenarbeit mit Ägypten und den USA bereits zu einem teilweisen Waffenstillstand und der Freilassung zahlreicher Gefangener und Geiseln gekommen sei. Die israelische Aggression habe dem Vermittlungsprozess zwar einen schweren Schlag versetzt, biete aber auch die Chance, arabische und internationale Positionen zu mobilisieren, um Druck auf die Besatzung auszuüben und ernsthafte Verhandlungen aufzunehmen, die zu einem Ende der Tragödie des Gaza-Krieges und einer umfassenden Lösung der Palästinafrage führen könnten.
Er fügte hinzu, der Erfolg dieser Bemühungen setze voraus, dass Katar seine feste Haltung beibehalte und die weitverbreitete Verurteilung der Aggression nutze, um internationale Unterstützung für Vermittlungsbemühungen und ernsthafte Garantien zu sichern, die die Besatzungsmacht dazu verpflichten, den Verhandlungsprozess nicht weiter zu untergraben. Dies könne der Gipfel von Doha mit arabischer und islamischer Unterstützung leisten.
Khaled Khalil, ein Experte für israelische Angelegenheiten, erklärte gegenüber der Qatar News Agency (QNA), der israelische Angriff auf eine Wohnanlage in Katar habe alle Grenzen überschritten und ein beispielloses Ausmaß an Kriminalität erreicht. Er betonte, dieser heimtückische und plötzliche Angriff auf den Vermittler und die Verhandlungspartei stelle einen gefährlichen kriminellen Präzedenzfall dar und schlage Alarm hinsichtlich der nationalen Sicherheit der arabischen und islamischen Welt, insbesondere der Golfregion, aus.
Khaled Khalil erklärte, dass das Ausmaß der Verbrechen Israels in Gaza und der Region direkt proportional zum Ausbleiben einer Reaktion der anderen Seite sei, was die Aktivierung der verfügbaren Abschreckungsinstrumente mit allen politischen, diplomatischen und wirtschaftlichen Mitteln erforderlich mache.
Er fügte hinzu, dass die Einberufung einer Dringlichkeitssitzung der Organisation für Islamische Zusammenarbeit, die 57 Länder umfasst und nach den Vereinten Nationen den größten politischen Block darstellt, einen grundlegenden Schritt zur Bekämpfung der Aggression darstelle, insbesondere da der Ministerrat der Organisation in den letzten Jahren eine herausragende politische Rolle übernommen habe.
Khalil ist überzeugt, dass es notwendig ist, Allianzen mit der Europäischen Union und westlichen Ländern zu schmieden, die zunehmend kritische Positionen gegenüber Israel einnehmen. Diese internationale Haltung soll genutzt werden, um Israel politisch, wirtschaftlich und diplomatisch zu bedrängen. Dies gilt insbesondere angesichts der zunehmenden Vorwürfe gegen Israel, im Gazastreifen Völkermord begangen zu haben, und der Entscheidung sechs europäischer Länder, innerhalb von weniger als zwei Wochen – zeitgleich mit den UN-Generalversammlungen – einen palästinensischen Staat anzuerkennen.
Khalil wies darauf hin, dass das Ausmaß der Unterstützung und Sympathie für Katar durch weitverbreitete Verurteilungen und zahlreiche Besuche islamischer Länder deutlich werde. Er betonte, dass Israel seine Verbrechen ungehindert fortsetzen werde, wenn es keine entschiedene Reaktion durch politischen und diplomatischen Druck erhalte.
Er fügte hinzu, die Ereignisse in Katar seien ein historischer Weckruf und unterstreiche die Notwendigkeit ernsthafter arabischer und islamischer Maßnahmen, die über bloße Erklärungen hinausgehen. Er wies darauf hin, dass die derzeitige israelische Führung extremistische ideologische Projekte unter dem Deckmantel biblischer und historischer Werte fördere und strategische und rationale Überlegungen außer Acht lasse. Dies sei ein selbstmörderischer Weg, der die Region in eine weitere Explosion führen werde.
Er betonte, dass der Angriff auf ein Hauptquartier der Hamas in Katar, einem diplomatisch aktiven Vermittler und einem der wichtigsten Verbündeten Washingtons außerhalb der NATO, eine gefährliche Entwicklung darstelle, die den arabisch-israelischen Konflikt neu aufflammen lasse, nachdem Israel versucht hatte, ihn auf einen bilateralen Streit zwischen sich selbst und den Palästinensern zu beschränken.
Er fügte hinzu, dass die Angriffe eine Schande für die extreme Rechte seien, die sich in das Schicksal der Region einmische. Katars Rolle liege darin, die notwendigen Instrumente zu aktivieren, um zu verhindern, dass sich die Aggressoren der Verantwortung entziehen. Zudem müsse Katar auf eine entschlossene, gemeinsame arabische Haltung drängen, um sicherzustellen, dass Israel nicht das Gefühl habe, vollendete Tatsachen geschaffen zu haben, und stattdessen neue Sicherheitsrealitäten schaffen müsse.
Khalil betonte, die gegenwärtige Phase biete eine historische Chance für arabische und islamische Länder, internationale Treffen zu nutzen, um Israel zu verurteilen, es für seine Verbrechen zur Rechenschaft zu ziehen und seine globale Isolation zu verstärken. Er betonte zudem die Notwendigkeit, die arabische und islamische Solidarität in konkrete, praktische Schritte umzusetzen, darunter den Schutz der Rechte des palästinensischen Volkes und die Wiederherstellung der palästinensischen Sache auf der internationalen Agenda.
Experten kommen zu dem Schluss, dass der Krisengipfel in Doha einen bedeutenden Meilenstein bei der Vereinigung arabischer und islamischer Positionen und der Umsetzung von Solidarität in konkrete praktische Schritte darstellt, darunter die Unterstützung der Standhaftigkeit des palästinensischen Volkes, die Einstellung der israelischen Angriffe auf Gaza und die Stärkung der Rolle Katars als zentraler und wirksamer Vermittler bei politischen und diplomatischen Vermittlungsbemühungen.
Analysten weisen darauf hin, dass der Angriff auf eine Wohnanlage in Katar die Position Katars nicht geschwächt, sondern ihre regionale und internationale Rolle gestärkt habe. Dies machte den Gipfel zu einer wichtigen Plattform für die Koordinierung der Reaktionen auf die israelische Aggression und die Aktivierung des politischen, diplomatischen und wirtschaftlichen Drucks auf Israel. Er gewährleistete den Schutz der Rechte des palästinensischen Volkes und betonte die Notwendigkeit, das Völkerrecht und die UN-Resolutionen einzuhalten.
(Enden)
a4558.en:
Damascus (UNA/QNA) - Syrian researchers and academics stressed that the Arab-Islamic emergency summit taking place on Monday in Doha underscores the importance of strengthening a unified Arab and Islamic stance towards the Israeli aggression that targeted the residential quarters of several Hamas leaders in the capital Doha. The aim, they said, is to confront Israel's aggressive policy, to strengthen support for the Palestinian people and their rights, and to highlight Qatar's central role in mediation efforts since the outbreak of the war.

In a statement to the Qatar News Agency (QNA), Dr Khaled Zaarour, Dean of the Faculty of Media at the University of Damascus, said that convening the summit at this moment has considerable implications. He pointed out that it took place immediately after the Israeli aggression against a Hamas residence in Doha, which is a clear indication of the significance of its timing and content.

He added: "At the summit there was unanimity in rejecting and condemning the aggression. It is regarded as a decisive turning point in the series of Israeli attacks, since it was directed against a country that is conducting negotiations and playing the role of mediator."

Dr Zaarour explained that the summit would send the message that unity prevails in Arab ranks and that the Arab heart is beating well.

He added that the aggression had had an impact on Arab and Islamic positions and had exposed the falsity of the Israeli reasoning by which the attacks were to be justified. He stressed that positions are not complete unless they are translated into practical steps. These include a complete political and economic boycott as well as a reshaping of military and political alliance plans, in order to find the most loyal and faithful allies and to use the economic power and geographic location of the Arab countries to strengthen their positions.

The Dean of the Faculty of Media at the University of Damascus noted that the aggression had been an attempt to weaken Qatar's role, but had in fact strengthened it. The statements of the Arab ambassadors before the UN General Assembly showed that Qatar had emerged from the aggression stronger and more influential, which will further strengthen justice for the Palestinian cause.

Dr Zaarour pointed out that the political and diplomatic response must focus on containing the aggressor and exposing its accusations, and not merely on preventing a repetition of the aggression.

Similarly, the political scientist Omar Idlebi of the Harmoon Center for Studies said that convening the emergency summit reflects a rare unity in the Arab and Islamic position and is a clear expression of solidarity with the State of Qatar in the face of an aggression that crosses all red lines.

Omar Idlebi explained that convening the summit after Qatar's political and diplomatic efforts and the international condemnations reflects the determination of the participating countries to coordinate their positions in order to confront Israel's aggressive policy towards the Palestinian people and other countries in the region, to highlight the suffering of the Palestinians in the West Bank, and to press the international community towards serious efforts to revive the two-state solution and the right of the Palestinian people to an independent state.

He added that the participating countries have various means of influence to achieve the desired goal. These include above all economic influence, in order to have a tangible effect on the international approach to regional problems and to end tolerance of the Israeli aggression.

He stressed that Qatari diplomacy had demonstrated a remarkable ability in dealing with the aggression. This was done through an official statement describing it as a blatant and treacherous attack, and through extensive diplomatic efforts in capitals and at the Security Council to mobilise support for Qatar's position. This led to the call for an Arab-Islamic summit to discuss and coordinate appropriate positions and responses and to support the Palestinian people in their confrontation with Israeli policy.

Idlebi explained that through Qatar's mediation, in cooperation with Egypt and the United States, a partial ceasefire and the release of numerous prisoners and hostages had already been achieved. The Israeli aggression had dealt a severe blow to the mediation process, but it also offers the chance to mobilise Arab and international positions in order to exert pressure on the occupation and to begin serious negotiations that could lead to an end to the tragedy of the Gaza war and a comprehensive solution to the Palestinian question.

He added that the success of these efforts presupposes that Qatar maintains its firm stance and uses the widespread condemnation of the aggression to secure international support for mediation efforts and serious guarantees obliging the occupying power not to further undermine the negotiation process. The Doha summit, with Arab and Islamic backing, could deliver this.

Khaled Khalil, an expert on Israeli affairs, told the Qatar News Agency (QNA) that the Israeli attack on a residential compound in Qatar had crossed all boundaries and reached an unprecedented level of criminality. He stressed that this treacherous and sudden attack on the mediator and negotiating party constitutes a dangerous criminal precedent and sounds the alarm regarding the national security of the Arab and Islamic world, particularly the Gulf region.

Khaled Khalil said that the scale of Israel's crimes in Gaza and the region is directly proportional to the absence of a response from the other side, which makes it necessary to activate the available instruments of deterrence by all political, diplomatic and economic means.

He added that convening an emergency session of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, which comprises 57 countries and constitutes the largest political bloc after the United Nations, represents a fundamental step in confronting the aggression, especially since the organisation's Council of Ministers has assumed a prominent political role in recent years.

Khalil is convinced that it is necessary to forge alliances with the European Union and Western countries, which are increasingly taking critical positions towards Israel. This international stance should be used to press Israel politically, economically and diplomatically. This applies in particular in view of the growing accusations against Israel of having committed genocide in the Gaza Strip, and the decision of six European countries, within less than two weeks - coinciding with the UN General Assembly sessions - to recognise a Palestinian state.

Khalil pointed out that the extent of support and sympathy for Qatar is evident from widespread condemnations and numerous visits by Islamic countries. He stressed that Israel will continue its crimes unhindered if it does not receive a determined response through political and diplomatic pressure.

He added that the events in Qatar are a historic wake-up call and underline the need for serious Arab and Islamic measures that go beyond mere declarations. He pointed out that the current Israeli leadership promotes extremist ideological projects under the cover of biblical and historical values and disregards strategic and rational considerations. This is a suicidal path that will lead the region into another explosion.

He stressed that the attack on a Hamas headquarters in Qatar, a diplomatically active mediator and one of Washington's most important allies outside NATO, represents a dangerous development that reignites the Arab-Israeli conflict, after Israel had tried to confine it to a bilateral dispute between itself and the Palestinians.

He added that the attacks are a disgrace to the far right, which is interfering in the fate of the region. Qatar's role lies in activating the necessary instruments to prevent the aggressors from evading responsibility. Qatar must also press for a determined, joint Arab position to ensure that Israel does not feel it has created a fait accompli, and must instead create new security realities.

Khalil stressed that the current phase offers a historic opportunity for Arab and Islamic countries to use international meetings to condemn Israel, hold it accountable for its crimes and intensify its global isolation. He also stressed the need to translate Arab and Islamic solidarity into concrete, practical steps, including protecting the rights of the Palestinian people and restoring the Palestinian cause to the international agenda.

Experts conclude that the Doha emergency summit represents a significant milestone in unifying Arab and Islamic positions and translating solidarity into concrete practical steps, including support for the steadfastness of the Palestinian people, an end to the Israeli attacks on Gaza, and the strengthening of Qatar's role as a central and effective mediator in political and diplomatic mediation efforts.

Analysts point out that the attack on a residential compound in Qatar did not weaken Qatar's position but strengthened its regional and international role. This made the summit an important platform for coordinating responses to the Israeli aggression and for activating political, diplomatic and economic pressure on Israel. It ensured the protection of the rights of the Palestinian people and stressed the need to comply with international law and UN resolutions.

(Ends)

Two analyses have captured Moscow’s battlefield struggles amid US-mediated talks to end the war.
Russia’s territorial gains in Ukraine are slowing down dramatically, two analyses have found, continuing a pattern from 2024 at a time when both nations are trying to project strength in the face of United States-mediated negotiations aimed at ending the war.
Britain’s Ministry of Defence last week estimated that Russian forces seized 143sq km (55sq miles) of Ukrainian land in March, compared with 196sq km (76sq miles) in February and 326sq km (126sq miles) in January.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
end of list
The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington, DC-based think tank, spotted the same trend, estimating Russian gains at 203sq km (78sq miles) in March, 354sq km (137sq miles) in February and 427sq km (165sq miles) in January.
These estimates are based on satellite imagery and geolocated open-source photography rather than claims by either side.
Should this trend continue, Russian forces could come to a standstill by early summer, roughly coinciding with US President Donald Trump’s self-imposed early deadline for achieving a ceasefire.
Russia’s diminishing returns have come even as it has greatly expanded the size of its forces from an estimated 150,000 soldiers who carried out its initial invasion in February to May 2022.
“Since the beginning of the aggression, the enemy has increased its group fivefold,” Ukrainian Commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskii told the online publication Livyi Bereg this week. He estimated that Russia has been adding 120,000 to 130,000 soldiers a year to its forces in Ukraine and it today has about 623,000 military personnel in the country.
Despite this, almost all of the Ukrainian territory Russia occupies, about a fifth of the country, was the result of the seizure of Crimea in 2014 and its initial, full-scale invasion in 2022.
A Ukrainian counteroffensive in 2023 took back about 20,000sq km (7,722sq miles). Russia has so far failed to recapture that.
Its grinding advances in Ukraine’s eastern region of Donetsk last year succeeded in wresting away just 4,168sq km (1,609sq miles) of fields and abandoned villages – equivalent to 0.69 percent of Ukraine, the Institute for the Study of War determined in January.
Those gains also came at a significant cost in men and materiel. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence put Russia’s losses of soldiers at 430,790. That’s the equivalent of 36 Russian motorised rifle divisions and outnumbers Russia’s losses in 2022 and 2023 combined.
While Russia has recruited enough soldiers to more than make up for its losses, its performance on the battlefield suggests it is struggling to train and equip its forces.
Moscow’s announcement of each capture, however small, has helped create an impression of inevitability to its conquest of Ukraine. On Monday, for example, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said it had taken the settlement of Katerinovka in Donetsk.
But these conquests have been small. The Institute for the Study of War estimated that even at 2024 rates of advance, Russia would have needed two years to capture the remaining parts of Donetsk alone. And that was before Russia’s pace of territorial gains slipped further in 2025.
Escalation with negotiation
Despite these trends, Russian President Vladimir Putin has escalated his aggression since US-Russian ceasefire talks kicked off on February 18.
An analysis by The Telegraph found that the number of Russian drone strikes against Ukraine rose by more than 50 percent from January to February.
In the first week of March, Russia launched a concerted effort that mostly pushed Ukrainian soldiers out of Kursk, a Russian border region Ukraine invaded in August.
On April 9, Russia said only two settlements – Gornal and Oleshnya – remained in Ukrainian hands in Kursk, and it was locked in fierce battles to recapture them.
Russia’s March success in Kursk coincided with a US intelligence and military aid cut-off for Ukraine.
During the past week, Russia was building up forces to follow up its success in Kursk by opening new fronts in Kharkiv and Sumy, two regions in northeastern Ukraine on the border with Russia, Syrskii said.
“For several days, almost a week, we have been observing an almost doubling of the number of enemy offensive actions in all main directions,” he said.
Syrskii also said he believed Russia could use joint military exercises with Belarus planned for the autumn as cover to mobilise more forces, a tactic Moscow used in late 2021. “The visibility of exercises is the most acceptable way to rebase, transfer troops, concentrate in a certain direction and create a troop group,” Syrskii said.
No ceasefire
Moscow also went on the diplomatic offensive this week, doubling down on efforts to vilify Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as an unreliable leader.
Russian officials said Ukraine was continuing to defy a ceasefire on energy infrastructure Kyiv never agreed to but that Moscow declared unilaterally on March 18 after a phone call between Trump and Putin.
On Friday, Russia’s Defence Ministry said Ukraine carried out half a dozen attacks on energy facilities in the Bryansk, Tambov and Lipetsk regions, causing gas outages to three cities and two electricity blackouts.
“More than 100 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles sent to bomb civilian targets on Russian soil in one night alone are a thousand times more telling than Zelensky’s wails about his ‘aspiration for peace’,” Russian special envoy Rodion Miroshnik wrote on his Telegram channel.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Monday said ceasefire negotiations were complicated by the “lack of control over the Kyiv regime, about the impossibility of the Kyiv regime to control the actions of a number of extremist and nationalist units that simply do not obey Kyiv”. That was a reference to the alleged existence of far-right elements in the Ukraine military.
Russia and the US are expected to hold a round of negotiations in Istanbul on Thursday.
On Wednesday, Russia’s Defence Ministry said two drones were shot down while trying to strike the gas distribution plant of the city of Temryuk, which sits on a neck of land on the Russian side of the Crimean Peninsula.
That same night, the ministry said, eight Ukrainian drones were shot down before reaching the Korenovskaya electrical plant, which powers the TurkStream gas pipeline. Ukraine has twice this year tried to shut the pipeline down by targeting its compressors.
In total, Russia’s Defence Ministry said it had intercepted 107 Ukrainian drones over 10 regions on the night of April 3 to early April 4 in one of the biggest such attacks.
But Russia, too, targeted the Kherson thermal power plant with a short-range first-person view (FPV) drone on Friday, Zelenskyy said. FPV drones generally carry up to 5kg (11lb), a much smaller payload than long-range strike drones, which usually ranges from 20kg to 50kg (44lb to 110lb).
The Kremlin gave less publicity to the fact that a Ukrainian drone barrage on Saturday struck the fibre optic systems plant in Saransk in Russia’s Mordovia. It is Russia’s only plant manufacturing optical fibre used in FPV drones and other defence systems.
Russia also did not mention that Ukrainian drones struck industrial explosives manufacturer Promsintez in the Samara region, causing 20 explosions and fires. The plant reportedly stopped production after the attack.
Syrskii said in his interview that drones had destroyed a $100m long-range Tupolev-22M3 bomber days earlier. Ukraine has targeted these bombers because they are used to launch thousands of glide bombs against Ukraine’s front lines every month.
Syrskii also said strikes against Russian airfields had pushed back the Russian air force, reducing its effectiveness.
Unlike Ukraine, which has consistently targeted defence and energy infrastructure, Russia has kept up long-range air attacks targeting Ukrainian cities.
In retaliation for Saturday’s attacks, Russia launched 18 cruise missiles, six ballistic missiles and 109 attack drones on Saturday night – its largest strike in a month.
Ukraine said it intercepted 93 of the drones, one ballistic and 12 cruise missiles but five ballistic missiles struck residential areas.
One of them killed 20 people in Kryvyi Rih, including nine children, prompting the United Nations Security Council to hold an emergency meeting.
“This is why the war must end,” US Ambassador to Kyiv Bridget Brink wrote on social media.
“Such a strong country, such a strong people – and such a weak reaction,” Zelenskyy responded on Telegram. “They are even afraid to say the word ‘Russian’ when talking about the missile that killed children.”
Russia accused Zelenskyy of deliberately framing the attack as an indiscriminate massacre of civilians whereas it was really targeting a meeting of foreign mercenaries with Ukrainian commanders at a restaurant.
But Russia followed up the ballistic missile strike in Kryvyi Rih with a wave of drones, which hit a playground and residential buildings.
Until this strike, Russia and Ukraine had observed an unofficial ceasefire over the Black Sea. This had apparently come to an end because Zelenskyy said several of the Russian missiles were launched from ships and submarines.
The attacks continued this week. Russia’s Defence Ministry on Monday said it shot down 19 Ukrainian drones overnight.
Ukraine’s air force said it intercepted 31 drones on Tuesday out of an attack totalling 46. The drones followed a strike by an Iskander ballistic missile in a tactic reminiscent of that on Kryvyi Rih.
The following night, Russia launched 55 Shahed drones at Ukraine. Ukraine’s air force said it downed 32 and disoriented eight. Russia said it downed 158 Ukrainian drones over 11 regions.

Ukraine’s 81st Separate Airmobile Sloboda Brigade on Tuesday said it captured two Chinese soldiers on Ukrainian soil.
Zelenskyy confirmed it at a news conference, saying, “Ukrainians engaged in combat with six Chinese service members in the Donetsk region – in Tarasivka and Bilohorivka.”
He later wrote on social media: “We have information suggesting that there are many more Chinese citizens in the occupier’s units.”
US Department of State spokesperson Tammy Bruce said Chinese soldiers’ involvement was “disturbing”.
Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Lin Jian on Wednesday denied Beijing’s involvement. But Russian television channels showed further evidence of Chinese troops in Ukraine weeks earlier.

Proche-Orient : Israël de nouveau accusé par l’Onu d’empêcher l’aide humanitaire
L’Office de secours et de travaux des Nations unies pour les réfugiés de Palestine dans le Proche-Orient (Unrwa) a de nouveau accusé le 5 février 2024, Israël d’avoir attaqué un convoi humanitaire. La mission onusienne précise que l’aide était destinée au Nord de la Bande de Gaza.
        
        
           
            
        C’est le direcreur de la mission, Thomas White qui en a fait l’annonce sur sa page X (Twitter). « Ce matin, un convoi de nourriture attendant d'entrer dans le nord de Gaza a été touché par des tirs navals israéliens - heureusement, personne n'a été blessé », a-t-il posté.
« Nous ne pouvons distribuer l’aide humanitaire sous les bombardements », a posté l’Unrwa sur sa page X (Twitter). Avant d’ajouter : « Un accès sûr et durable à l’aide humanitaire est nécessaire d’urgence partout, y compris au nord de Gaza ».
Le post du patron de l’Unrwa fait l’objet de nombreux commentaires favorables sur les réseaux sociaux. Jasmin (@JsmnMA) fait partie des soutiens de la mission onusienne et qualifie les dirigeants de l’État Hébreu de « nouveaux Nazis ».
En face, des internautes expriment leur rejet de l’accusation portée contre la marine israélienne. Middle East: Israel again accused by the UN of obstructing humanitarian aid

The United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) again accused Israel, on 5 February 2024, of having attacked a humanitarian convoy. The UN mission specifies that the aid was destined for the north of the Gaza Strip.

It was the director of the mission, Thomas White, who made the announcement on his X (Twitter) page. “This morning, a food convoy waiting to enter northern Gaza was hit by Israeli naval gunfire — fortunately, no one was injured,” he posted.

“We cannot distribute humanitarian aid under bombardment,” UNRWA posted on its X (Twitter) page. Before adding: “Safe and sustained access to humanitarian aid is urgently needed everywhere, including in northern Gaza.”

The post by the head of UNRWA is the subject of numerous favourable comments on social media. Jasmin (@JsmnMA) is among the supporters of the UN mission and describes the leaders of the Hebrew State as “the new Nazis”.

On the other side, internet users express their rejection of the accusation made against the Israeli navy. Arsen Ostrovsky (@Ostrov_A) asks: “How do you know it was Israeli naval fire? Did you see it yourself? Do you have proof? Can you also demonstrate that Hamas was not operating near the convoy?”

NYT: The United States will withdraw support from countries where it was not originally planned to stop aid
NEW YORK, April 10. /tass/. The administration of US President Donald Trump has cut aid programs for several countries where it initially promised to maintain support. This was reported by The New York Times (NYT) newspaper with reference to the lists provided to officials and staff of humanitarian organizations.
According to these lists, the United States will stop funding programs in Afghanistan, Jordan, Yemen, Iraq, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Lebanon, Madagascar, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Syria, Somalia, Chad and Ecuador. The Reuters news agency, citing sources, reported on April 9 that the White House later decided to restore payments under the World Food Program (WFP) in Lebanon, Syria, Somalia, Jordan, Iraq and Ecuador.
According to WFP estimates, Washington's refusal to provide assistance will have the greatest impact on Afghanistan, where about 2 million people, including 400,000 children, depend on food supplies. The population of Yemen, where 2.4 million people receive food as part of humanitarian programs, will also suffer.
NYT interlocutors at the US Agency for International Development (USAID) stressed that they often learn about the termination of another program directly from humanitarian organizations that stop receiving funding.
In early February, Trump suspended the activities of USAID, which allocated a significant amount of funds to finance international organizations. Later, the US administration announced its intention to cancel 92% of the agency's and the State Department's aid contracts. On March 10, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was previously appointed interim head of USAID, announced that the US government had officially terminated 83% of the agency's programs following a six-week audit. According to him, within the framework of 5,200 contracts that were canceled, tens of billions of dollars were spent not in the interests of the United States, and in some cases to their detriment.

a5284.t:
By: Maltiti Sayida Sadick
Hailemariam Desalegn Boshe, the former Prime Minister of Ethiopia and current board chair of Trademark Africa, recently highlighted the slow pace of intra-Africa trade, which currently accounts for just 15% of the continent’s total trade. Speaking at a summit hosted at the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Secretariat in Accra, Ghana, Desalegn underscored both the progress and the challenges Africa faces in fostering regional trade integration.
Despite the continent’s significant strides in economic integration, Desalegn pointed out the stark contrast in intra-regional trade compared to other continents, such as Asia, where intra-regional trade stands at over 50%. He noted that while Africa’s total merchandise exports surged by 200% between 2017 and 2023, intra-Africa trade only increased by 27% during the same period, growing from $140 billion to $190 billion.
“The political commitment to AfCFTA is strong, and we are beginning to see more African goods being exchanged,” Desalegn remarked, emphasizing that trade under the AfCFTA has become more encouraging, especially between 2017 and 2023. He also lauded the progress made toward the formation of a single African market, describing the launch of the AfCFTA five years ago as a landmark moment for the continent.
With a population of 1.2 billion people and a combined GDP of $3 trillion, Desalegn stressed that the potential for economic growth and prosperity through increased regional trade is immense. However, he also pointed out the long-standing challenges that continue to hinder trade within Africa, including inadequate trade infrastructure and colonial-era legacy systems that were not designed for regional integration.
“We have seen the export of raw materials like gold, cocoa, and coffee, only for these to return to Africa as processed goods. Our infrastructure, built by colonial powers, remains a major barrier to implementing AfCFTA fully,” he explained.
The COVID-19 pandemic further disrupted trade flows in Africa, exacerbating the difficulties faced by businesses and governments alike. Nevertheless, Desalegn emphasized the importance of Africa navigating these challenges carefully to ensure the successful implementation of AfCFTA and its long-term objectives.
The AfCFTA, which was scheduled to be fully implemented in 2020, promises to eliminate tariffs on 97% of tariff lines across member states over a specified period. Desalegn, who played a key role in the formation of the African Union’s Agenda 2063, recognized the historical importance of the AfCFTA and acknowledged the anticipated challenges, but remained optimistic about the future.
“While there have been frustrations along the way, the achievements of AfCFTA remain undeniable,” he stated. “Africa’s exports are projected to grow faster than any other region, with the World Trade Organization forecasting a 5.3% increase in 2024, up from 3.1% in 2023.”
In conclusion, Desalegn expressed confidence in the future of African trade integration, citing the commitment of African nations to the AfCFTA agreement and the growing momentum toward creating a unified, more interconnected market. He urged governments, businesses, and regional bodies to continue working together to overcome the obstacles and fully realize the economic potential of the AfCFTA.

a5351.t:
Niamey,10 mars(ANP)-Le président du Conseil National pour la Sauvegarde de la Patrie (CNSP), Chef de l’État, le général de brigade Abdourahamane Tiani, a reçu, ce lundi 10 mars 2025, le rapport final des assises nationales au palais présidentiel.
Après 18 jours de travaux, la commission nationale, conduite par le Dr Mamoudou Harouna Djingarey, Chef de canton de Sinder, a remis officiellement le rapport au président du CNSP.
Ce dernier a exprimé sa reconnaissance et sa gratitude envers tous ceux qui ont contribué, de près ou de loin, à ces assises.
Il a également salué le travail accompli par l’équipe ayant mené ces consultations nationales.
Le président Abdourahamane Tiani a souligné que « aujourd’hui, nous recevons les copies des mains du président ayant conduit les assises nationales. Gardons à l’esprit que ce n’est plus le moment des rancœurs, des divisions ou de l’adversité stérile. Tout ce que nous devons faire doit s’inscrire dans la défense et la préservation des intérêts du Niger, ce Niger sans lequel nous n’aurions pas de raison d’être. Ce Niger que nous avons le devoir de défendre au prix de nos vies, nous y parviendrons, mais nous y parviendrons ensemble. Aucun pays ne se développe dans la division, aucun pays ne se développe dans un esprit de clan, aucun pays ne se développe sans cohésion sociale ni esprit de construction collective. »
Le Chef de l’État a également rappelé que »ceux qui n’avaient pas encore eu la possibilité de participer pouvaient le faire dans les trois semaines à venir. Je crois que ce délai était suffisant pour permettre à tous d’apporter leur contribution. Il s’agit des intérêts du Niger, et ces intérêts sont au-dessus de toute appartenance, de tout individualisme et de tout clanisme. Il faut que le Niger existe pour que les intérêts particuliers puissent subsister,Travaillons pour l’existence de notre pays, particulièrement en cette période difficile. »
Le général de brigade Abdourahamane Tiani de souligner également que « nous faisons face à une insécurité que nous avons toujours qualifiée d’importée. Il est de notre responsabilité de mettre fin à cette importation de l’insécurité dans notre Sahel, afin qu’il devienne un espace de prospérité pour l’ensemble des peuples qui y vivent, plutôt qu’un espace d’insécurité car qui dit insécurité dit misère, dit pertes en vies humaines . Les intérêts défendus à travers cette insécurité ne sont pas des intérêts nationaux, que ce soit pour le Mali, le Burkina Faso ou le Niger. »
MAY/AS/ANP 050 mars 2025
a5351.en:
Niamey, 10 March (ANP) - The President of the National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland (CNSP), Head of State, Brigadier General Abdourahamane Tiani, received the final report of the national consultations (assises nationales) at the presidential palace this Monday, 10 March 2025.

After 18 days of work, the national commission, led by Dr Mamoudou Harouna Djingarey, chief of the Sinder canton, officially handed the report over to the President of the CNSP.

The latter expressed his appreciation and gratitude to all those who contributed, directly or indirectly, to these consultations.

He also praised the work accomplished by the team that conducted these national consultations.

President Abdourahamane Tiani stressed that "today, we receive the copies from the hands of the president who led the national consultations. Let us keep in mind that this is no longer the time for resentment, division or sterile hostility. Everything we do must be part of the defence and preservation of the interests of Niger, this Niger without which we would have no reason to exist. This Niger which we have a duty to defend at the cost of our lives; we will get there, but we will get there together. No country develops in division, no country develops in a clan spirit, no country develops without social cohesion or a spirit of collective construction."

The Head of State also recalled that "those who had not yet had the opportunity to take part could do so within the next three weeks. I believe that this period was sufficient to allow everyone to make their contribution. It is about the interests of Niger, and those interests are above any affiliation, any individualism and any clannishness. Niger must exist for particular interests to be able to survive. Let us work for the existence of our country, particularly in this difficult period."

Brigadier General Abdourahamane Tiani also stressed that "we are facing an insecurity that we have always described as imported. It is our responsibility to put an end to this importation of insecurity into our Sahel, so that it becomes a space of prosperity for all the peoples who live there, rather than a space of insecurity, because insecurity means misery, means loss of human life. The interests defended through this insecurity are not national interests, whether for Mali, Burkina Faso or Niger."

MAY/AS/ANP 050 March 2025
