Niamey, 06 Juin (ANP) – À l’occasion de la célébration de l’Aïd Al-Adha, communément appelée la fête de Tabaski, ce vendredi 6 juin 2025, les autorités nigériennes ont transmis leurs salutations distinguées à la Oumma Islamique du Niger.
A cette occasion, le ministre de l’intérieur de la sécurité publique et de l’administration du Territoire, le Général de Division Mohamed Toumba a saisi l’opportunité pour adresser ses vœux à la population nigérienne et au-delà.
« Il nous incombe de présenter nos vœux les plus sincères à l’occasion de cette célébration de la fête de Tabaski à la population nigérienne et à l’ensemble de la communauté islamique » a-t-il déclaré tout en exprimant sa »gratitude au Tout-Puissant qui nous a permis de célébrer cette fête dans des bonnes conditions et de bénéficier de sa grâce pour atteindre l’année prochaine dans des circonstances encore plus favorables ». »Nous profitons de cette occasion pour remercier une fois de plus l’ensemble du peuple nigérien pour son engagement et son soutien au CNSP afin que nous puissions ensemble célébrer dignement la fête de Tabaski « , a-t-il poursuivi.
Le ministre de l’intérieur, de la sécurité publique et de l’administration du Territoire a, par la suite, fait savoir que » le moment est venu de relever notre pays et de l’orienter véritablement vers le développement. Vous avez sans doute suivi l’entretien que Son Excellence le Président de la République, Chef de l’État, a bien voulu accorder il y a quelques jours. Lors de cet échange, il a exposé la situation que nous traversons « .
Aujourd’hui, a-t-il fait remarquer, » il n’est plus un secret pour personne que ce que nous vivons est véritablement historique. Nous nous trouvons à une période charnière de notre existence. Nous devons faire face à cette situation avec toute la détermination nécessaire. C’est une situation que vous percevez clairement, empreinte de nombreux dangers » notant, en effet, que lorsque »l’on se retrouve seul à lutter contre les forces impérialistes, il est indéniable que la tâche s’avère ardue ».
« Ce sont ces mêmes nations qui produisent l’armement, qui nous fournissent les équipements militaires, et qui, par moments, entravent également notre accès à ces ressources, nous empêchant ainsi d’assurer notre sécurité. Nous devons faire preuve de discernement et d’une analyse approfondie dans nos actions quotidiennes, tout en appelant la population à collaborer « , a souligné le général de Division Mohamed Toumba.
Il a une fois de plus exprimé ses vœux pour une bonne fête à la population et présenté ses condoléances aux familles endeuillées des victimes des attaques terroristes, » rendons hommage aux martyrs et se souvenir d’eux dans les moments difficiles est légitime pour exprimer la gratitude envers ceux qui ne sont plus parmi nous « .
Quant au gouverneur de la région de Niamey, le Général de Division Assoumane Abdou Harouna, il a saisi l’occasion pour adresser ses vœux de fête à l’ensemble de la population de la région de Niamey et au-delà, à tout le peuple nigérien.
« Rendons grâce à Dieu, le Clément, le Miséricordieux, qui nous a permis de nous retrouver une fois de plus en ce jour de célébration de la fête deTabaski », a-t-il dit avant de rappeler qu’il y a »quelques semaines, le gouvernement a pris des mesures judicieuses pour empêcher l’exportation du bétail. Cela visait à éviter une flambée des prix, phénomène que nous avons l’habitude de constater chaque fois que la fête approche. Cela a également permis à chaque Nigérien, en fonction de ses moyens, d’acquérir un mouton.Dans l’ensemble, nous pouvons affirmer que cette mesure a porté ses fruits. Vous pouvez observer l’engouement qui règne un peu partout. »
« Nous aspirons donc à ce que cette fête d’Aïda Al-Adha soit des plus belles.Je souhaite également profiter de vos ondes pour aborder, dans le même sens que le président de l’association islamique, l’appel qu’il a formulé à l’endroit du peuple nigérien, incitant à des comportements positifs ».
»La recherche de la cohésion sociale, de l’unité nationale et de comportements fraternels est primordiale » a-t-il soutenu.
»Vous avez également suivi l’interview du chef de l’État il y a quelques jours, au cours de laquelle il a salué le sursaut patriotique du peuple nigérien lors de l’initiation de notre refondation « .
« Ensemble, dans un esprit d’unité nationale et de cohésion sociale, construisons notre avenir dans l’esprit de la Confédération AES. C’est une nouvelle dynamique qui a été insufflée pour que nos interlocuteurs apprennent à nous respecter, à nous prendre en considération et qu’ils abandonnent les comportements de mépris et de condescendance qu’ils ont pu avoir à notre égard » a souhaité le gouverneur de Niamey pour qui »ce narratif négatif, qu’ils ont porté sur nous, doit être compris par l’ensemble du peuple nigérien afin que, collectivement, nous bâtissions le Niger de la refondation ».
MAM/AS/ANP 030 juin 2025
a7440.en:
Niamey, 06 June (ANP) - On the occasion of the celebration of Eid al-Adha, commonly called the Tabaski festival, this Friday 6 June 2025, the Nigerien authorities conveyed their distinguished greetings to the Islamic Umma of Niger.

On this occasion, the Minister of the Interior, Public Security and Territorial Administration, Major General Mohamed Toumba, took the opportunity to address his wishes to the Nigerien population and beyond.

"It falls to us to extend our most sincere wishes on the occasion of this celebration of the Tabaski festival to the Nigerien population and to the entire Islamic community," he declared, while expressing his "gratitude to the Almighty who allowed us to celebrate this festival in good conditions and to benefit from his grace to reach next year in even more favourable circumstances." "We take this opportunity to thank once again the entire Nigerien people for their commitment and their support for the CNSP so that together we may celebrate the Tabaski festival with dignity," he continued.

The Minister of the Interior, Public Security and Territorial Administration then made it known that "the time has come to lift up our country and truly steer it towards development. You have no doubt followed the interview that His Excellency the President of the Republic, Head of State, was kind enough to grant a few days ago. During that exchange, he set out the situation we are going through."

Today, he pointed out, "it is no longer a secret to anyone that what we are living through is truly historic. We find ourselves at a pivotal period of our existence. We must face this situation with all the necessary determination. It is a situation you perceive clearly, marked by many dangers," noting indeed that when "one finds oneself alone in fighting against the imperialist forces, it is undeniable that the task proves arduous."

"It is these same nations that produce the weaponry, that supply us with military equipment, and that, at times, also obstruct our access to those resources, thus preventing us from ensuring our security. We must show discernment and thorough analysis in our daily actions, while calling on the population to cooperate," stressed Major General Mohamed Toumba.

He once again expressed his wishes for a good festival to the population and offered his condolences to the bereaved families of the victims of terrorist attacks: "let us pay tribute to the martyrs; remembering them in difficult moments is legitimate in order to express gratitude towards those who are no longer among us."

As for the Governor of the Niamey region, Major General Assoumane Abdou Harouna, he took the occasion to address his festival wishes to the entire population of the Niamey region and beyond, to the whole Nigerien people.

"Let us give thanks to God, the Clement, the Merciful, who has allowed us to come together once again on this day of celebration of the Tabaski festival," he said, before recalling that "a few weeks ago, the government took judicious measures to prevent the export of livestock. This was aimed at avoiding a price surge, a phenomenon we are used to seeing every time the festival approaches. It also allowed each Nigerien, according to his means, to acquire a sheep. Overall, we can affirm that this measure has borne fruit. You can observe the enthusiasm reigning just about everywhere."

"We therefore aspire for this Eid al-Adha festival to be the most beautiful. I would also like to take advantage of your airwaves to address, in the same vein as the president of the Islamic association, the appeal he made to the Nigerien people, encouraging positive behaviour."

"The pursuit of social cohesion, national unity and fraternal behaviour is paramount," he maintained.

"You also followed the Head of State's interview a few days ago, during which he hailed the patriotic surge of the Nigerien people at the initiation of our refoundation."

"Together, in a spirit of national unity and social cohesion, let us build our future in the spirit of the AES Confederation. It is a new dynamic that has been instilled so that our interlocutors learn to respect us, to take us into consideration, and to abandon the attitudes of contempt and condescension they may have had towards us," wished the Governor of Niamey, for whom "this negative narrative, which they have carried about us, must be understood by the entire Nigerien people so that, collectively, we build the Niger of refoundation."

MAM/AS/ANP 030 June 2025

a7492.t:
Dr. Tony Okpanachi, Managing Director/CEO, Development Bank of Nigeria (DBN), in this interview with SYLVESTER ENOGHASE, speaks on how the bank has provided long-term finance to support over 60 Primary Financial Institutions (PFIs) since its inception, to address the challenges confronting Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), in Nigeria. Excerpts:
You spent some decades working in commercial banks before heading a development bank. Since its creation, what impact has the DBN had on the plans to diversify the economy?
It has been interesting coming from strictly commercial focus of profitability to impacting lives through providing access to credit for MSMEs which results in job creation, empowerment, economic growth and diversification.
On DBN, it is a wholesale Development Bank with three specific mandates: Increase access to finance for MSMEs by lending to Participating Financial Institutions (Commercial Banks, Micro Finance Banks and other DFIs) for on-lending to this segment; Provide Capacity Building for Participating Financial Institutions to enhance their ability and willingness to lend to the MSME segment and Provide Partial Credit Guarantees for Participating Financial Institutions to encourage them to take the risk of lending to MSMEs.
DBN has provided long-term finance to over 60 Primary Financial Institutions (PFIs) since its inception. This is to address challenges confronting Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in the country. And our lending model is sustainable, quota-blind
DBN, for instance as at December 2022, for instance had provided N631 billion as financing support to the PFIs, while over 313,000 MSMEs had benefited from the support which led to the creation of more than 900,000 jobs.
Also, on women empowerment and gender equality, women-owned MSMEs accounted for 69 per cent of all businesses financed by the end of the 2022 financial year.
The bank continued to catalyse growth across key and various sectors, changing the dynamics of development in the country.
The trade and commerce sector in Nigeria, for instance, accounts for the highest number of micro-businesses and informal enterprises within the country
According to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), more than 80 per cent of the entire population of Nigeria, which is more than 160 million Nigerians, depends on the informal economy.
This means that the trade and commerce sector is the hope of daily survival and livelihood for most Nigerian families and entrepreneurs
The management of DBN recognised this critical need and thereby channelled N230 billion to support small businesses in the trade and commerce sector over the past five years, leading up to December 2022.
The manufacturing sector contributed between 12 per cent to 17 per cent to the national economy over the past three to five years and it remained one of the highest labour-intensive sectors.
DBN also supported MSME players in the manufacturing sector with more than N69 billion in financing.
Our bank recognises the significance of agriculture in the country’s economy and has allocated substantial funding to agro-MSMEs which is crucial for improving food security in Nigeria.
DBN provided N27 billion to Agro-MSMEs which played a vital role in supporting agricultural activities, empowering farmers, and promoting agro-entrepreneurship.
Would you agree that development banks in Nigeria are failing in their mandate?
No. This is because the concept of development finance institutions is not a new phenomenon.
They have been used all over the world as instruments of economic growth and infrastructural development.
What makes development financial institutions (DFIs) succeed or fail is the model – the pattern through which the intervention funds are made available to the sector where they are required.
This is not to deny that there are instances where the development funds haven’t reached the end beneficiaries due to ineffective distribution channels however, in the case of DBN, there was a very deliberate calibration to avoid the pitfalls of defective DFIs while embracing the principles of successful ones.
This led to the creation of DBN premised on the PFI lending model, which offers a more sustainable path to MSME financing through established channels and competitive pricing.
It is our belief that if DFIs follow this pattern, there will be an increase in their effectiveness and eventual outcome.
In the case of DBN, we have facts to show the sustainability and effectiveness of our lending model in gender balance
Are you saying that DBN have confidence in in creating an ecosystem with gender parity?
Yes. The Development Bank of Nigeria believes strongly in the importance of creating an ecosystem with gender parity where everyone has an equal opportunity to prove his/her role and contribute to societal development.
The Nigerian women have proven over the years how resourceful and dependable they can be, and in some cases have paid the ultimate price for the good of others.
For us at DBN, we celebrate our females as well as remember our fallen heroines, in the likes of great personalities like Dr. Stella Ameyo Adadevoh, Prof. Dora Akunyili, Tolulope Arotile, Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti to mention a few, who have been inspirational, not just to women but to the world at large.
In its continuous bid to ensure compliance with the Nigerian Sustainable Banking Principles which also aligns with the United Nation’s Sustainable Development Goals, the DBN is committed to continue to lend its voice to gender equality and empowerment.
What is your take on the recent World Bank’s international debt report which shows poorest countries face risk of debt crises as borrowing costs surge?
The recent World Bank’s international debt report indicated that developing countries amid the biggest surge in global interest rates in four decades spent a record $443.5 billion to service their external public and publicly guaranteed debt in 2022
The increase in costs shifted scarce resources away from critical needs such as health, education, and the environment in developing countries.
The debt-service payments which include principal and interest from the report increased by 5 percent over the previous year for all developing countries, while the 75 countries eligible to borrow from the World Bank’s International Development Association (IDA)—which supports the poorest countries paid a record $88.9 billion in debt-servicing costs in 2022.
It became obvious that interest payments by these countries over the past decade, have quadrupled, to an all-time high of $23.6 billion in 2022, while the overall debt-servicing costs for the 24 poorest countries are expected to balloon in 2023 and 2024 by as much as 39 percent.
We are worried that the record debt levels and high interest rates have set many countries on a path to crisis while every quarter that interest rates stay high results in more developing countries becoming distressed and facing the difficult choice of servicing their public debts or investing in public health, education, and infrastructure.
The situation warrants quick and coordinated action by debtor governments, private and official creditors, and multilateral financial institutions more transparency, better debt sustainability tools, and swifter restructuring arrangements as the alternative is another lost decade.
What about the high interest rates?
The surging interest rates have intensified debt vulnerabilities in all developing countries because in the past three years alone, there have been 18 sovereign defaults in 10 developing countries greater than the number recorded in all of the previous twodecades.
It is on record that about 60 percent of low-income countries are at high risk of debt distress or already in it.
This is because the interest payments consume an increasingly large share of low-income countries’ export as more than a third of their external debt, moreover, involves variable interest rates that could rise suddenly.
It is also on record that most of these countries face an additional burden: the accumulated principal, interest, and fees they incurred for the privilege of debt-service suspension under the G-20’s Debt Service Suspension Initiative (DSSI).
Well, the stronger US dollar is adding to their difficulties, making it even more expensive for countries to make payments because under the circumstances, a further rise in interest rates or a sharp drop in export earnings could push them over the edge.
As debt-servicing costs have climbed, new financing options for developing countries have dwindled because in 2022, new external loan commitments to public and publicly guaranteed entities in these countries dropped by 23% to $371 billion the lowest level in a decade.
While the Private creditors largely abstained from developing countries, receiving $185 billion more in principal repayments than they disbursed in loans and that marked the first time since 2015 that private creditors have received more funds than they put into developing countries.
And the new bonds issued by all developing countries in international markets dropped by more than half from 2021 to 2022, and issuances by low-income countries fell by more than three-quarters. New bond issuance by IDA-eligible countries fell by more than three-quarters to US$3.1 billion.
It is also on record that with financing from private creditors drying up, the World Bank and other multilateral development banks stepped in to help close the gap.
The multilateral creditors provided $115 billion in new low-cost financing for developing countries in 2022, nearly half of which came from the World Bank , and through IDA, the World Bank provided $16.9 billion more in new financing for these countries than it received in principal repayments nearly three times the comparable number a decade ago.
In addition, the World Bank disbursed $6.1 billion in grants to these countries, three times the amount in 2012.
There is a school of thought that says the MSME financing has always been an issue in Nigeria. Can we say the creation of DBN is proving the school of thought wrong?
Yes. MSMEs are, collectively, the largest employers in many low-income countries including Nigeria, yet their viability is being threatened by lack of access to risk-management tools such as savings, insurance and credit.
Indeed, their growth is often stifled by restricted access to credit, equity and payments services.
Fortunately, the global pursuit of financial inclusion as a vehicle for economic development has had a positive impact in Nigeria to some degree as the exclusion rate reduced from 53 per cent in 2008 to 46.3 per cent in 2010.
Encouraged by this positive development, the Central Bank of Nigeria in collaboration with stakeholders launched the National Financial Inclusion Strategy (NFIS) on 23rd October 2012 aimed at further reducing the exclusion rate to 20% by 2020.
Further to this, the Development Bank of Nigeria (DBN) was conceived by the Federal Government of Nigeria in collaboration with the World Bank, African Development Bank, German Development Bank (KfW), French Agency for Development and European Investment Bank to address the major financing challenges facing Micro, Small and Medium Scale Enterprises (MSMEs) in Nigeria.
Development Bank of Nigeria provides sustainable financing through eligible Participating Financial Institutions (PFIs), who would in turn, lend to end-borrowers – Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs).
Today, that concept is an operational entity. DBN obtained its Wholesale Development Banking license in March 2017.
Our approach is a simple and easy-to-access on-lending model which allows for scale and broader reach as we provide support working through Participating Financial Institutions (PFIs).
Is there any specific status that DBN is focusing on?
That is the unique thing about DBN. It is not status specific, but we are overtime going to encourage some growth sector to be able to ensure that it is in line with the development objective.
So, we are going to encourage some growth sectors, but as we speak, we don’t have specific sector.
The key thing for us is that whatever sector of the economy you are, the questions are, are you able to create employment? Are you able to empower people? And all these things will help in diversification of the economy, which are the developmental impact you want to make in the economy. That is what we are focusing on, but that does not mean that with time, we will not begin to encourage some growth sectors to ensure that they are be able to make more meaningful impact.
The International Monetary Fund recently raised its 2023 global growth estimates slightly given resilient economic activity in the first quarter, but warned that persistent challenges were dampening the medium-term outlook. What is your take on this?
The IMF in its latest World Economic Outlook said inflation was coming down and acute stress in the banking sector had receded, but the balance of risks facing the global economy remained tilted to the downside and credit was tight.
The global lender from its report projected global real GDP growth of 3.0% in 2023, up 0.2 percentage point from its April forecast, but left its outlook for 2024 unchanged, also at 3.0%.
The 2023-2024 growth forecast remains weak by historical standards, well below the annual average of 3.8% seen in 2000-2019, largely due to weaker manufacturing in advanced economies, and it could stay at that level for years.
The report indicated that new technologies could boost productivity in coming years, but that in turn could be disruptive to labor markets.
The outlook is “broadly stable” in emerging market and developing economies for 2023-2024, with growth of 4.0% expected in 2023 and 4.1% in 2024
But, it noted that credit availability is tight and there was a risk that debt distress could spread to a wider group of economies as forces that hindered growth in 2022 persist, citing still-high inflation that was eroding household buying power, higher interest rates that have raised the cost of borrowing and tighter access to credit as a result of the banking strains that emerged.
The impact of higher interest rates , according to the report was especially evident in poorer countries, driving debt costs higher and limiting room for priority investments.
As a result, output losses compared with pre-pandemic forecasts remain large, especially for the world’s poorest nations
How do you see the current picture of development finance of Africa, the second-largest continent and home to over one billion people that has long captured the imagination of the world?
Development finance of Africa has its limitations in amounts available, acceptable repayment risk and in some cases; financing cost vs project viability.
In addition, such finance often comes with strictures on how African nations should run their economies.
As such, solutions that are imported rather than developed at home may inadvertently come at a hefty price.
This is a legacy of the post-World War II era, when extraordinary efforts to provide provisional financial and technical assistance to European countries in the wake of the war’s devastation helped to set them back on the path to national unity.
Since then, this approach’s foundations have become the cornerstone of development thought.
But, there’s no denying that the traditional development finance model has not worked for Africa over the past six decades. Even though the world economy has grown in the past few decades, commodities in most African nations are highly susceptible to market fluctuations and natural disasters, and their societies are prone to instability, making it difficult to attract foreign investment. That is why most African nations turn to development aid to survive, which is not a viable model to achieve sustainable economic development. For instance since 1990, African countries have received over $1.3 trillion in development assistance; however, the continent’s financial, societal, and political fabric remains fragile.

Consumers will experience significant relief at pharmacy counters nationwide as prices of pharmaceutical products have been reduced by a substantial 5 to 15 per cent across the board.
This will ease the financial burden on consumers and support government’s efforts to stabilise the economy.
This was announced in a joint statement by the Ghana National Chamber of Pharmacy (GNCoP) and the Pharmaceutical Importers and Wholesalers Association (PIWA) yesterday (June 4).
The statement commended the government for the recent measures that have led to a marked and sustained appreciation of the cedi against major foreign currencies, particularly the US dollar.
Impact
It said the cedi's appreciation has provided relief to the pharmaceutical sector, which relied heavily on imports for active pharmaceutical ingredients, finished pharmaceutical products, medical consumables, and equipment.
“It said a stronger cedi means lower foreign exchange costs for pharmaceutical importers, resulting in lower prices for essential medicines and health products,” it said.
It further explained that currency stability allowed for better forecasting, planning, and pricing, particularly important for small and medium pharmaceutical enterprises.
It added that with reduced cost pressures, pharmacies and hospitals were now better positioned to stock essential medicines, contributing to improved public health outcomes.
It said “while we acknowledge these recent gains, it is important to note that the sector has, over the period absorbed a huge percentage of the cost due to the depreciation of the cedi.”
The statement said many businesses were holding old stocks procured at higher rates, and the financial burden on importers and distributors remains considerable.
“However, in support of government efforts to stabilise the economy and reduce inflation, and in the interest of the public health and consumer welfare, GNCoP in consultation with PIWA have resolved to reduce their prices by 5-15 per cent across the board.
This decision is a demonstration of our sector’s commitment to national development and public health.”
Commitment
The statement said government must continue its prudent economic management and maintain support for the private sector, especially the pharmaceutical industry, which played a critical role in ensuring medicine security and public health resilience.
"We remain hopeful that this stability will be sustained in the long term.
“The Chamber & PIWA also reiterate its commitment to working collaboratively with the government and all stakeholders to ensure the pharmaceutical sector remains vibrant, accessible, and sustainable for the benefit of all Ghanaians,” it added.
